tldr: In online RL using large pretrained robot models as priors, this work proposes a geometric support behavior regularization that imposes zero penalty inside the base policy's support and a smooth distance penalty outside. This enables discarding suboptimal modes while allowing fine-grained refinement, boosting the average success rate from 33% to 95%.
hero_caption: The procedure of GSBR for geometrically relaxing the support of actions. Reference samples are drawn from the base policy, and an adaptive radius $r_{\mathcal{B}}$ is computed from local sample spacings to build a union of balls $C$. Actions inside this region incur zero regularization penalty, while actions outside face a penalty proportional to the minimum distance $d(a, C)$.
overview:
Trial-and-error from scratch is prohibitively expensive when running online reinforcement learning (RL) on physical robots or high-fidelity simulators. A popular approach is to leverage pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models or diffusion policies as behavioral priors to guide exploration. However, while base policies trained on massive datasets exhibit diverse skills, they also contain suboptimal modes unnecessary for a specific downstream task, leaving their standalone performance insufficient.

This introduces a fundamental dilemma in behavioral regularization: how should we guide the RL agent? Standard behavioral cloning (BC) or KL regularization pulls the actor toward the full distribution of the base policy, preventing it from pruning away failure-prone modes (mode averaging). Conversely, hard support constraints strictly forbid actions outside the non-zero probability region (support) of the base policy, blocking the agent from making local improvements that lie just outside the support boundary.

This paper proposes Geometric Support Behavior Regularization (GSBR), resolving this trade-off with an elegant geometric formulation. GSBR levies zero penalty within the support region of the base policy, allowing the agent to freely select promising high-value modes. Outside the support, instead of an infinite hard barrier, it applies a finite penalty based on the Euclidean distance to the region. This enables the agent to safely venture just beyond the support boundary for local refinement whenever the expected Q-value gain outweighs the penalty.

Evaluated across 19 tasks on four major robotic benchmarks, GSBR boosts the average success rate from 33% (for the base policy) to 95%. Furthermore, in terms of normalized throughput—measuring successful completions per unit time—GSBR outperforms the next-best RL method by about 23%, setting a new state of the art.
contributions: Proposed Geometric Support Behavior Regularization (GSBR), which simultaneously enables selecting promising modes from a base policy (mode selection) and fine-tuning actions beyond the support boundary (local refinement).

Introduced a practical method to approximate the unknown support region using an adaptive radius derived from nearest-neighbor distances among finite samples, supported by theoretical convergence guarantees.
Demonstrated top performance across 4 robotic benchmarks (19 tasks), improving the base policy's success rate from 33% to 95% and outperforming existing RL methods by roughly 23% in throughput.

sections.heading: The Dilemma of Using Large Models as Priors in Online RL
sections.summary: While base policies are indispensable for constraining exploration in robot online RL, existing regularizers face severe trade-offs. Distribution-matching methods fail to discard suboptimal modes, whereas hard support constraints cannot reach optimal actions outside the support. This work resolves the dilemma through a geometric relaxation that penalizes actions outside the support smoothly with distance.
sections.details:
Online reinforcement learning (RL) on physical robots has a very high trial cost. Therefore, leveraging pretrained behavioral priors to guide exploration has become standard practice. Today, Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and World-Action Models (WAM) trained on extensive demonstration datasets provide a broad repertoire of skills. However, they often lack sufficient reliability and throughput out of the box, necessitating online RL fine-tuning.

To improve upon a base policy, an online RL agent requires two critical capabilities:

- Mode selection: For example, in a scene with two objects where the base policy exhibits modes to grasp either, the agent must completely discard the mode reaching for the wrong object and concentrate solely on the correct one.
- Local refinement: The ability to adjust an action slightly outside the base policy's repertoire, such as correcting minor grasp misalignment, to discover better behaviors.

Unfortunately, existing behavioral regularizers hinder at least one of these capabilities. Distribution matching methods, such as action regression (e.g., TD3+BC) or KL regularization, bind the actor to the base policy's entire distribution, penalizing it even for pruning low-value modes. On the other hand, hard support constraints (e.g., BEAR, DSRL) permit mode selection but strictly forbid actions outside the support, preventing local refinement to optimal actions located just beyond the boundary.

To break this impasse, the authors introduce a geometric relaxation of support constraints. By imposing zero penalty inside the support covered by the base policy and applying a smooth, distance-dependent penalty only outside it, the actor can freely pick high-value modes within confident regions and safely step outside to refine its behavior whenever the critic's value gain exceeds the penalty.

sections.heading: How Prior Methods Were Constrained by Base Policies
sections.summary: Online RL methods using base policies either update the diffusion model parameters directly or freeze them and train an auxiliary actor. For the latter, coordinating the actor with the base policy is critical; existing distribution matching, hard support constraints, and residual RL methods all suffer from limitations in flexibility.
sections.details:
This section organizes related research streams and clarifies how GSBR differs from existing approaches.

### Sample-Efficient Online RL
Off-policy actor-critic methods improve sample efficiency through experience replay, replay buffer strategies, and demonstration data. GSBR is orthogonal to these techniques and enhances efficiency further by combining a frozen pretrained model as an exploration prior.

### RL with Generative and Diffusion Policies
Approaches that improve diffusion or flow-matching policies via RL fall broadly into two categories. One directly updates the parameters of the generative model using RL policy gradients. The other freezes the large base policy and trains a lightweight auxiliary actor to modify its outputs or guide latent noise. GSBR belongs to the latter. It avoids backpropagating gradients into the base model weights and can handle any black-box policy as long as it provides sample access.

### Taxonomy of Action Constraints and GSBR's Position
Behavioral regularizers in prior work can be categorized into three main paradigms:

- Distribution matching and action regression: Pull the actor toward the base policy's mean or overall distribution, causing mode collapse (averaging across distinct modes) or forcing the retention of suboptimal modes.
- Support constraints: Allow free selection within the base policy's support, but strictly prohibit venturing outside, preventing local refinement.
- Residual RL: Add learned corrections to the base policy output. However, conventional residual RL (e.g., EXPO) sets fixed uniform bounds on the residual magnitude regardless of the base policy's distribution shape. DICE-RL uses a distance penalty, but it penalizes distance to specific sample points, continually pulling the actor backward and restricting free movement within the support.

In contrast, GSBR explicitly approximates the support region itself from reference samples and sets zero penalty across the entire region. This design simultaneously achieves genuine mode selection and flexible, distance-regularized local refinement.

sections.heading: Problem Formulation: How to Leverage a Base Policy
sections.summary: This work optimizes a policy using finite samples from a frozen base policy alongside offline and online transition datasets. The actor receives the current state and reference actions, learning to balance Q-value maximization against a behavioral regularization loss.
sections.details:
This section outlines the problem setting and mathematical formulation.

### Online RL with Behavioral Priors
The problem is modeled as a standard Markov Decision Process (MDP). The learner has access to a frozen, pretrained base policy $\pi_{\beta}$ and an offline transition dataset $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{off}}$ composed of task-specific demonstrations. It learns a policy using a replay buffer $\mathcal{D}$ that mixes offline data with online interaction data $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{on}}$. Crucially, the method assumes only sample access to $\pi_{\beta}$—generating action samples $b \sim \pi_{\beta}(\cdot \mid s)$ given state $s$—without requiring access to its internal parameters or gradients.

### Three Core Challenges
This setup presents three fundamental difficulties:

- $\pi_{\beta}$ is multimodal, with different modes yielding vastly different values.
- Computing the exact support of the base policy is intractable due to high dimensionality and complex generative structures.
- The critic $Q_\phi$ is trained on limited data and is prone to overestimating values for unvisited actions outside the data distribution, which the actor might exploit.

### Actor-Critic Framework
The actor $\pi_\theta(\cdot \mid s, \mathcal{B})$ takes as input both the state $s$ and a set of $N$ reference actions $\mathcal{B} = \{b_1, \ldots, b_N\}$ drawn from the base policy. The critic $Q_\phi(s,a)$ is trained via standard temporal difference errors. Meanwhile, the actor is updated to maximize the regularized objective:

$$\max_\theta \; \mathbb{E}\left[ Q_\phi(s, \pi_\theta(s, \mathcal{B})) - \alpha \, \ell_{\mathrm{beh}}(\pi_\theta(s, \mathcal{B})) \right]$$

where $\ell_{\mathrm{beh}}$ is the behavioral regularization penalty, and $\alpha$ controls its strength. Designing an effective $\ell_{\mathrm{beh}}$ is the key determinant of learning performance.

sections.heading: How GSBR Works: Zero Penalty Inside Support, Distance Cost Outside
sections.summary: GSBR estimates an ideal geometric relaxation loss adaptively from a finite set of reference samples. It derives an adaptive radius from the quantile of nearest-neighbor distances between samples, forming the support region as a union of balls. The paper provides theoretical proofs showing convergence to the true geometric loss as the sample size increases.
sections.details:
This section presents the mathematical formulation and concrete algorithm of GSBR.

### 4.1 Geometric Relaxation of Support Constraints
Let $S_{\beta}(s)$ denote the true support of the base policy. The ideal regularization loss $\ell_{\mathrm{supp}}$ is defined using the Euclidean distance $d(a, S_{\beta}(s)) = \inf_{b \in S_{\beta}(s)} \|a - b\|_2$ from an action $a$ to the set $S_{\beta}(s)$:

$$\ell_{\mathrm{supp}}(a) = d(a, S_{\beta}(s))^2$$

When action $a$ is inside the support, the distance is zero, incurring no penalty. The actor is therefore free to concentrate on whichever mode has the highest Q-value, regardless of the base policy's original sampling frequency. Conversely, outside the support, the penalty grows quadratically with distance. This permits safe exploration outside the support boundary only when the Q-value improvement exceeds the penalty.

### 4.2 Support Approximation via Reference Action Neighborhoods
In practice, $S_{\beta}(s)$ cannot be computed analytically. The challenge is estimating the support using only a finite sample set $\mathcal{B} = \{b_1, \ldots, b_N\}$. Simply penalizing the distance to individual sample points would penalize actions falling in the spaces between samples, pulling the actor toward specific discrete points.

To address this, GSBR defines balls centered at each sample point and takes their union as the estimated support region $C$. Rather than fixing the radius $r_{\mathcal{B}}$, GSBR determines it adaptively based on local sample density. Specifically, for each sample $b_i$, it computes the nearest-neighbor distance $u_i = \min_{j \neq i} \|b_i - b_j\|_2$ to other samples and sets the radius to its $q$-quantile:

$$r_{\mathcal{B}} = \mathrm{Quantile}(\{u_1, \ldots, u_N\}, q)$$

Using a quantile $q \in (0, 1)$ filters out extreme outlier distances from isolated samples in low-density regions, automatically tuning the radius to the internal density of major modes. Over the resulting support region $C$, the GSBR regularization loss is computed cleanly as:

$$\ell_{\mathrm{GSBR}}(a, \mathcal{B}) = \left[ \min_{b \in \mathcal{B}} \|a - b\|_2 - r_{\mathcal{B}} \right]_+^2$$

where $[x]_+ = \max(x, 0)$. This intuitive, computationally lightweight formula simply measures the distance to the nearest reference sample, subtracts $r_{\mathcal{B}}$, and penalizes only the positive surplus quadratically.

### Theoretical Guarantees (Theorem 4.1)
Under standard assumptions of a compact action space and continuous density functions, the paper rigorously proves that $\ell_{\mathrm{GSBR}} + 2Dr$ upper-bounds the true loss $\ell_{\mathrm{supp}}$, and that the estimator converges uniformly in expectation to the true loss as the number of samples $N \to \infty$.

captions.F2: Conceptual diagram of GSBR support region estimation. (a) Reference actions are sampled from the base policy; (b) nearest-neighbor distances between samples are measured to determine the adaptive radius $r_{\mathcal{B}}$; (c) the support region $C$ is constructed as the union of balls of radius $r_{\mathcal{B}}$ centered at each sample. The agent moves penalty-free within the region, while optimal actions outside can still be reached at a finite distance-based cost.

sections.heading: Evaluation Across 19 Tasks: Superior Success Rates and Throughput
sections.summary: GSBR was evaluated against seven baselines across 19 tasks spanning RoboMimic, OGBench, OCBench, and LIBERO. GSBR achieved an average success rate of 95% (compared to 33% for the base policy) and outperformed the next-best method by 23% in normalized throughput. Ablation studies confirmed that the adaptive radius plays a crucial role in maintaining performance.
sections.details:
This section details comprehensive comparative experiments and ablations conducted in simulation environments.

### 5.1 Experimental Setup
The evaluation covers 19 tasks across four diverse benchmark suites:

- RoboMimic: 4 tasks featuring human demonstrations, requiring precise alignment and bimanual coordination (such as tool-hang).
- OGBench: Long-horizon tasks with diverse exploratory data (5 variants of cube-triple), testing the agent's ability to prune irrelevant modes.
- OCBench: 5 realistic tasks mimicking the statistical properties of human demonstrations.
- LIBERO: 5 vision-based (pixel input) tasks using a pretrained VLA model, $\pi_{0.5}$-LIBERO, as the base policy.

GSBR is benchmarked against seven strong methods: TD3+BC (action regression), RLT (reference chunk conditioning), Residual Policy (residual RL), BFN (sample selection via Q-maximization), DSRL (latent exploration in noise space), EXPO-FT (bounded residual with test-time selection), and DICE-RL (selective BC-regularized residual). Each task was evaluated across 50 episodes over 3 random seeds.

### 5.2 Key Results
Across all 19 tasks, while the base policy achieved an average success rate of only 33%, GSBR achieved an impressive 95% (compared to 92% for the second-best baseline, RLT).
More notably, in terms of normalized throughput—measuring successful completions per unit time to reflect both task success and efficiency—GSBR achieved 0.95, outperforming RLT's 0.77 by roughly 23%.

- On OGBench, where the strong baseline RLT scored an 86% success rate and 0.75 throughput, GSBR dominated with a 100% success rate and 1.00 throughput. This highlights the effectiveness of its clean mode selection in discarding unhelpful behaviors.
- On LIBERO with a VLA base policy, GSBR attained an 85% success rate and 0.86 throughput, matching or exceeding the top-performing baselines.

### Ablations and Visualizations

- Effect of support radius $r_{\mathcal{B}}$: Setting $r_{\mathcal{B}}=0$ (penalizing raw Euclidean distance to sample points) caused normalized throughput on cube-triple to plummet from 1.0 to 0.66. Providing penalty-free balls around samples is critical.
- Sensitivity to sample count $N$: Throughput remained stable at 1.0, 0.91, and 0.93 for $N=8, 16, 32$, showing that as few as 8 reference samples provide robust regularization.
- Support visualization: Comparing the estimated support against true kernel density estimates (KDE) from 5,000 samples revealed that with just $N=8$, GSBR accurately captures both primary modes while leaving the low-density valley between them penalized.

The suite spans precise tool hanging, long-horizon block manipulation, and image-based VLA control.

Even with only $N=8$ samples, the two modes are accurately covered. The learned actor action (star) lies just outside the support, showing successful local refinement with minimal penalty.
captions.F6: Learning curves showing throughput (successes per hour) over training steps across 19 benchmark tasks. GSBR (brown line) rapidly outpaces baseline methods (blue lines) in both learning speed and peak throughput on most tasks.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Directions
sections.summary: GSBR introduces a practical online RL regularization approach that geometrically relaxes the base policy's support, balancing mode selection with local refinement. While limitations include test-time sampling latency and an extra hyperparameter, extending this method to physical robot deployments represents an exciting next step.
sections.details:
This work tackled a core challenge in online RL with behavioral priors: providing stable guidance without overly restricting policy optimization. GSBR offers a conceptually simple, theoretically grounded geometric solution. Extensive experiments across 19 tasks proved that it dramatically increases base policy success rates from 33% to 95%, while surpassing existing RL methods in throughput by 23%.

The authors also discuss several limitations and future research avenues:

- Test-time sampling cost: Generating multiple reference samples from the base policy during inference adds computational overhead and increases execution latency.
- Additional hyperparameter: Computing the adaptive radius introduces the quantile parameter $q$, although the method remains robust across a wide range of values.
- Lack of physical robot validation: Experiments were conducted exclusively in simulation benchmarks; validating GSBR on real-world robotic hardware is a natural next step.

sections.heading: Appendix: Implementation Details and Sensitivity Analysis
sections.summary: The appendix details practical implementation techniques that stabilize training, including action chunking, 50% reference dropout, and pessimistic ensembles with 10 Q-functions. Grid searches further verify that GSBR is robust across a wide range of hyperparameters.
sections.details:
This section covers practical implementation choices and analyses from Appendix A.1, A.2, and A.4.

### Key Implementation Techniques

- Action chunking: Both the base policy and the RL actor predict sequences of $H$ consecutive actions (ranging from 3 to 10 steps depending on the task). Executing an entire chunk before predicting the next ensures smooth motion and enables long-horizon consistency.
- Reference action conditioning and dropout: The actor conditions on $N$ reference actions $\mathcal{B}$, but reference dropout is applied with 50% probability during training. This prevents the actor from lazily memorizing or copying the reference actions.
- 50/50 demonstration sampling: Replay buffer minibatches are sampled evenly (50:50) from offline demonstration data and online rollout data, preventing policy collapse during early learning.
- Pessimistic targets with 10 Q-networks: An ensemble of 10 critic networks is trained in parallel. Target Q-values subtract the standard deviation from the ensemble mean, implementing pessimistic evaluation that effectively suppresses overestimation on unvisited actions.

### Hyperparameter Sensitivity Analysis
Grid search evaluations across regularization weight $\alpha$ and radius quantile $q$ showed that GSBR maintains consistently high success rates and throughput over broad parameter ranges. Notably, performance remained stable across $q \in [0.1, 0.9]$, demonstrating that the method does not require tedious hyperparameter tuning for practical deployment.

captions.F7: Heatmaps displaying grid search results over regularization weight $\alpha$ and quantile $q$ across OCBench tasks. High success rates (left column) and throughput (right column) are maintained over a broad hyperparameter range, demonstrating strong robustness.

takeaways: When using large models as behavioral priors, geometric relaxation—imposing zero penalty inside the support and a distance-based penalty outside—is far more effective than pulling toward the full distribution.
The unknown geometry of the base policy's support can be accurately approximated with as few as 8 samples by setting adaptive radii based on nearest-neighbor spacings.
Measuring normalized throughput, which accounts for execution efficiency alongside success rates, is essential for evaluating practical robotics RL.
limitations: Drawing multiple reference samples from the base policy during inference increases computational overhead and action latency.
Introduces the nearest-neighbor distance quantile $q$ as an additional hyperparameter, even though sensitivity to this parameter is low.
Empirical evaluation was conducted entirely within simulated environments (RoboMimic, OGBench, OCBench, LIBERO) without real-world physical robot verification.
